I am 62 years old, and I have been farming these flat fields in Quzhou County for more than forty years. I only finished primary school, but I know this land and this climate better than any book. On the North China Plain, there is only one sensible way to farm if you want to feed your family and have grain left to sell: the winter wheat–summer maize double crop. I have 8 mu of good farmland, and I will plant all of it to wheat this October, then follow immediately with maize next June.

For the winter wheat, I will sow **Jimai 22**, an improved variety that has done well for my neighbors and me—steady yields, and it does not lodge easily. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to break up the soil and bury the maize stubble from last summer. I will put down a basal compound fertilizer and then top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. Wheat needs water at the right moments, so I will irrigate four times using water from my well and border irrigation: at sowing if the soil is dry, once over winter if it turns too dry, once at green-up, and once at heading. For pests, I will spray herbicide once, insecticide twice, and fungicide once if I see rust appearing.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will not waste a single day. I will plant **Denghai 605**, a hybrid maize, directly into the wheat stubble with no tillage. Time is short before autumn, and no-till saves fuel and labor. Maize does not need as much fertilizer as wheat, so I will apply compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress once with urea when the plants are knee-high. I will irrigate twice—at the big trumpet stage and again at tasseling—and spray herbicide once and insecticide twice for corn borers. If the weather cooperates as it usually does, I expect about 1,000 kg of wheat per mu and about 1,100 kg of maize per mu.
